title: The North Face Rock 22 review: a sturdy two-door tent for solo or couples
dek: Three 9 mm DAC poles, two doors, two vestibules and a five-minute pitch. Owners say it's tough and good value, with condensation in the cold.
subject: The North Face Rock 22
verdict: The Rock 22 is a sturdy, roomy, good-value two-door tent that owners trust in rain and wind, including 70 mph gusts when fully guyed out. It's heavy for backpacking, collects frost in freezing weather, and the vestibules are small. For car camping or short hikes it's an easy recommendation used.
bestFor: Solo campers who want room, couples car camping, scouts and families on a budget.

body:
## The short version

The Rock 22 is a three-pole, two-door, two-vestibule tent that owners describe as sturdy, roomy and good value. It's been discontinued, but plenty are still in use, and owners mention versions in green-and-beige and salmon-and-beige from around 2007 to 2010.

## Weather

Many owners say it stayed dry in heavy rain and strong wind, and one reports it standing up to 70 mph gusts once it was staked and guyed out. A few found the fly let water in during hard sideways rain.

## Condensation

The mesh walls keep it cool on hot nights. In freezing weather, frost and condensation build on the fly and can drip inside. One owner advises against using it below about 25°F.

## Space and setup

Solo, it's very roomy. Two adults fit, with gear in the vestibules. The gear loft takes some headroom, which taller people notice. Setup takes under five minutes with color-coded clips, though one owner notes the poles can slide at the top without a tie-down.

## Upgrades owners recommend

Swap the stock stakes, which most owners call flimsy. Watch the vestibule zipper in rain, since it faces up and lets water in when you open it.

## Poles and parts

The Rock 22 uses **3 poles**, **9 mm** tubing, **DAC aluminum**.

The Rock 22 and Rock 32 both use 9 mm poles, but the Rock 32's floor is bigger, so don't assume their poles are interchangeable. Check length and sections.

The North Face doesn't publish pole lengths. To match a replacement, lay your pole out straight, measure tip to tip, count the sections, and read the diameter printed near a joint (or use calipers). Then search the Rock 22 in our [pole and parts finder](/poles?model=Rock%2022), compare against measured stock in the [pole size chart](/poles/sizes), or search by measurement in [find a pole by size](/poles/size).

## Bottom line

A used Rock 22 is a tough, easy tent for car camping and short trips. Backpackers chasing low weight will want something lighter.
